title: The Second Balance Sheet: Why a Family's Investment Vehicle Rarely Gets the Discipline of the Business That Funded It
linkedin:
Ask most family principals what their investment vehicle actually returned last year, and the honest answer is usually that nobody has calculated it.

A lot of successful owner-led businesses on the East Coast quietly become two entities over ten or fifteen years. The trading business keeps its discipline because it has no choice, payroll, BAS, the bank wanting a management pack before it renews a facility. The investment vehicle sitting next to it, the trust, the holding company, the property, the share portfolio, answers to none of that. It gets looked at once a year, usually at tax time, usually by the accountant preparing the return rather than anyone asking whether the capital inside it is actually working.

The cost of that gap is real even when nothing looks obviously wrong. Capital sits concentrated in one asset because nobody has compared it against the alternatives. A related-party loan quietly funds the trading business's working capital at no interest, which flatters the business's numbers while masking what the investment side is giving up.

That gap tends to surface at the worst possible time, a succession conversation, a sale, a family member wanting their share out. By then the questions are years overdue.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog. Link in the first comment.

Genuine question for anyone running a family business alongside a property or share portfolio built from its profits.

When did you last actually check what that second entity is earning?

Most owner-led businesses on the East Coast end up with two balance sheets over time, the trading business, and everything built alongside it. The business gets monthly attention because payroll and the bank demand it. The investment side usually gets looked at once a year, at tax time, by whoever is preparing the return rather than anyone asking if the capital in it is actually working hard enough.

It is rarely a disaster waiting to happen. It is just years of decisions made on habit rather than on a proper look at the numbers.

Worth ten minutes this week if it has been a while. #familybusiness

A useful check for business owners across Brisbane, the Gold Coast and further afield who have built more than the trading business over the years.

A lot of successful owner-led companies end up with a second structure alongside them, a trust, a holding company, a property or share portfolio, funded out of profit from the business itself. The business keeps its financial discipline because payroll, BAS and the bank all force the issue every month. The investment side next to it often does not get that same attention. It tends to get reviewed once a year, at tax time, rather than checked regularly for whether the capital inside it is actually earning what it should.

That is not a criticism of anyone's bookkeeping. It is simply what happens when one entity has a forcing function for regular review and the other does not. The cost shows up quietly, capital sitting in one asset for years without comparison, a related-party loan nobody has revisited, a governance decision made informally that the next generation was never part of.

If your family has built wealth alongside the business as well as through it, it is worth applying the same rigour to both. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
